chapter_theme: Neelakesi worships at the Jina's shrine, whose doors open on her oath of right faith, and sings eight hymns that praise the omniscient one by paradox and by his victory over deeds, death and birth; she then chooses the Buddha's teaching as the first mean path to crush, sees by clairvoyance Kundalakesi's unanswered challenge-branch at the gate of Kampili, flies there in a woman's form, learns from the gatekeeper why the gate is barred, and plucks up the branch.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Arhat, the Jain omniscient teacher, worshipped in the shrine and addressed in the hymns
the Buddhist woman debater whose challenge-branch stands at the gate of Kampili
the gatekeeper of the king of Kampili
the king of Kampili, before whose assembly the debate is to be held

150.reading: Carrying flowers without limit, from the mullai, konku, kurundham, kanthal, kuravam and jasmine of the garden to the cool many-petalled kuvalai, paanal and paathiri, she rises to go to the Lord's place.
150.event: Neelakesi gathers every kind of flower and sets out for the Lord's shrine.
150.nuance: The sarukkam opens with worship, not argument: the debater's first act is to bring flowers, and the list runs through flowers of forest, garden and water alike.

151.reading: She takes in the shrine's height, length and breadth, circles it, and declares that if her vision does not stray from the lord of great penance every door shall open; they open, and she bows at the feet of the lord who rules the three worlds.
151.event: Neelakesi swears by her unswerving faith in the Jina, the shrine's doors open of themselves, and she worships at his feet.
151.nuance: காட்சி (line 3) is the word for right vision or faith, the first of the three jewels in Jain teaching; the doors open on an oath sworn by it, so the verse makes her right faith, not a priest or a key, the thing that admits her. The verse narrates the oath and its effect; it does not state the efficacy of right faith as a rule.

152.reading: With fine flowers worked into figures of rare skill, elephants, yalis, wild cattle, the eight auspicious signs, rows of images, birds, creepers and trees, she offers worship at the holy feet of the one who gave the good path of the perfected.
152.event: Neelakesi worships the Jina's feet with flowers arranged in pictures of animals, birds and the eight auspicious signs.
152.nuance: The Jina is named by what he gave, சித்த நன்னெறி, the good path of the siddhas (the released), not by any act of creation or rescue.

153.reading: With incense, sandal and scented powder she praises and bows, hangs garlands, and in wonder at the form of the seer of the tattvas strings good songs on the thousand and eight names and sings them to melody.
153.event: Neelakesi offers incense and garlands and sings hymns on the Jina's thousand and eight names.
153.nuance: ஆயிரத்தோர் எண் நாம (lines 3 and 4) is read as the thousand and eight names, a Jain litany of the Jina as other traditions have theirs; the eight hymns that follow (154 to 161) are presented as these songs. Line 3 (யாமென றையென வியந்து) is obscure in this text and its sense is not fixed.

154.reading: Neelakesi sings that the Jina passed beyond angry Death, drove off Kama of desire, renounced ancient aging and crossed the great sea of birth, and that disease and enmity broke together on the battlefield while he stood the victor, hero of heroes.

claims.claim: the Jina has passed beyond death, desire, aging and birth

154.nuance: The victory is told in a battle image (வெங்களத்து, வென்றிருந்தனை, வீரர்தம் வீரர்க்கும் வீரா), but every enemy named is inward or a condition of embodied life; the Jina wins by leaving them behind (கடந்தாய், துறந்தாய், இறந்தாய்), not by striking them.

155.reading: She sings that for all the souls who suffer in the sea of evil deeds they themselves did, through death, disease, aging and birth, the Jina gave a good path free of harm and made the raft that is hard to find, poet of poets.

claims.claim: souls suffer birth, aging, disease and death in a sea made of the evil deeds they themselves did
the Jina's teaching is the raft by which souls cross that sea

155.nuance: The sea is தாம் செய் தீவினைக் கடல், the sea of the evil deeds the souls did themselves: no one else is blamed for their suffering, and the Jina's part is to make the raft (புணை படைத்தாய்), not to carry anyone. Line 3 (திரைசெய் நீள்கரை ஒருவி) is read as leaving the wave-beaten shore behind.

156.reading: She sings that after rare wonders, with the gods beating drums and raining flowers, he sat in the shade of the spreading asoka tree within the circle of golden walls and taught the way by which the two kinds of deed part from the soul.

claims.claim: the Jina taught the way by which both good and evil deeds are separated from the soul

156.nuance: The setting is the Jain preaching assembly: the golden ring of walls (பொன் எயில் மண்டிலம்), the asoka tree (பிண்டி), the drums and the rain of flowers. What is taught is that both deeds (இருவினையும்) part, so good deeds too must go for release; the Jina states the way and the soul must walk it.

157.reading: She sings that with yakshas waving whisks on either side, seated on the lion throne under the halo and the three moon-white umbrellas, he proclaimed the Angas and the Purvas so that the gods' assembly understood, knower of knowers.

claims.claim: the Anga and Purva scriptures were proclaimed by the omniscient Jina himself

157.nuance: அங்க பூவம் names the two classes of Jain canon, the Angas and the Purvas; the verse grounds the scripture's authority in the omniscient speaker, which is the ground the later sarukkams use against the Veda.

158.reading: She sings a set of paradoxes: he perceives no touch yet tells the kinds of touch, never says 'I will speak' yet has a voice like a drum, has no wish to harm yet sets his feet on flowers; how is she to understand him, god of gods.

claims.claim: the omniscient one knows the objects of the senses without perceiving them through the senses

158.nuance: Each line sets a lack beside a power: knowledge without sense-contact, speech without intention, walking on flowers without the will to hurt them. The third paradox concerns ahimsa: the Jina's steps fall on flowers, yet no harm is meant. Line 2 is elliptic, and the reading supplies 'yet speaks'.

159.reading: She sings that he sees nothing with the eye yet sees all things at once, joins with no woman yet has undivided great bliss, eats nothing yet has a radiant form, so that no one who thinks can know him, lord of lords.

claims.claim: the omniscient one sees all existing things together without the eye
the omniscient one takes no food yet keeps a radiant body

159.nuance: Line 3 (உண்ணல் யாவதும் இலையாய்) says the omniscient one does not eat. Whether the omniscient being eats was disputed among Jains themselves, and this verse takes the side that denies it; the hymn states it as praise, not as an argued position. The bliss of line 2 is பிரிதலில் பேரின்பம், bliss that does not part, set against the joy of union with a woman.

160.reading: She sings that he hears no word yet utters the scripture and its certain conclusions, has learned nothing yet knows endless things, clings to nothing yet has the spread-out eightfold wealth; who can fully know him, first of the first.

claims.claim: the omniscient one's knowledge of all things is not acquired by hearing or learning

160.nuance: சுதநயம் (line 1) joins the Jain terms for scripture (சுதம், sruta) and standpoint (நயம், naya). The 'eightfold wealth' of line 3 is read as the eight splendours that attend the Jina, such as those 157 lists, held without attachment (பற்று).

161.reading: She sings that his true knowledge, which he set out in words, proves false what the other teachers each said from what they knew; none of them has discerned it, and who else knows his nature that burns the whole chain of deeds, leader of leaders.

claims.claim: the other teachers spoke only from what each partly knew, and their teachings are false
the Jina's knowledge burns away the whole chain of deeds

161.nuance: The last of the eight hymns turns from praise to the rival teachers, and so prepares the debate. The burning of deeds belongs to the Jina's own nature and knowledge (நின் ஞானம், நின் தன்மை); the verse does not say he burns the deeds of others.

162.reading: Having bowed at the holy feet of the Arhat, who is beyond measure of beginning and end, with great praise in his shrine full of dharma, she sits and asks which of the many mean paths she should crush first.
162.event: After worship Neelakesi sits in the shrine and asks herself which rival path to overthrow first.

claims.claim: the other religious paths are base paths to be overcome

162.nuance: She calls the other schools புன்னெறி, mean paths, before hearing any of them; the debates that follow are set up as a campaign (அடர்க்கற்பாலது, to be crushed) begun at the Jina's feet.

163.reading: Neelakesi decides: the Buddha does not call eating flesh a fault, does not say the soul exists, and does not count enduring austerity as a vow; his mean path robs people like courtesans with alluring eyes, and her task is to go and bring it down.
163.event: Neelakesi chooses the Buddha's teaching as the first she will overthrow.

claims.claim: eating flesh is not a fault
enduring bodily austerity is not a vow

163.nuance: This is a Jain's summary of Buddhism, and two of its charges are framed as silences (என்னான், he does not say). The work answers them later: on flesh in the Mokkala sarukkam (342, 347), on the soul in Neelakesi's reply to Kundalakesi (194 to 202). The charge about austerity is not answered in the passages read, so it is left as reported. The comparison to courtesans who cut the purse (பொதியறுக்கும்) is polemic; a Buddhist would not accept that the teaching despoils its hearers.

164.reading: Looking over the land by her far-seeing knowledge, she sees that at the gate of the king of Kampili a naaval branch has been planted in the cool grove and stands unanswered, and she takes the name of Kundalakesi as her mark.
164.event: By clairvoyance Neelakesi sees the unanswered challenge-branch planted at the gate of the king of Kampili and takes Kundalakesi as her opponent.
164.nuance: அவதி (line 1) is the Jain term for clairvoyant knowledge, one of the grades of knowledge below omniscience. A naaval (rose-apple) branch planted at a king's gate is the debater's challenge; உரைபெறா says no one has answered it.

165.reading: She who never swerves from dharma, so as to do an act of compassion, circles the great city made in the ordained manner, meditates on the perfected ones on the holy pearl seat, and takes the form of a woman like a great pearl.
165.event: Neelakesi circles the holy city, meditates on the siddhas and takes a woman's form to go to the debate.
165.nuance: The purpose of the debate is given as தயா செய்தல், doing compassion: refuting a school is framed as mercy toward those it misleads. The sentence runs on into 166. 'The city made in the ordained manner' (நிருமித்த வகையினதா நெடுநகர்) and the pearl seat may be the Jina's assembly rather than an earthly city; the reading is not fixed.

166.reading: Going by the sky, she reaches the palace of the king who is an Indra among spear-bearing kings and tells the gatekeeper she is a Gandharva maiden who wants to see the king, and that he should announce her quickly.
166.event: Neelakesi flies to Kampili and asks the gatekeeper to announce her to the king as a Gandharva maiden.
166.nuance: She gives the gatekeeper a false identity (கந்திருவ மகளேன், I am a Gandharva's daughter); the narrative lets the disguise stand without comment.

167.reading: The gatekeeper replies that elephants and horses stand crowded at their posts and stalls and cannot go to water, chariots are not yoked, and not even the great army comes to the long gate, because of the sinful woman who planted a tree and sits here; so it is hard for him to let her in.
167.event: The gatekeeper explains that the gate has been closed and the palace traffic stopped since a woman planted a challenge-branch there.
167.nuance: The planted branch closes the king's gate itself: until someone answers the challenge, the palace's elephants, horses and chariots cannot pass. The challenger is called பெண்பாவி, sinful woman, by the gatekeeper, not by the narrator.

168.reading: Hearing him and looking at his face, the sharp-eyed one asks what grievance keeps her from the palace, offers to set things right, and asks whether there is a quarrel, a loss of property or a loss of life here, and what the cause is.
168.event: Neelakesi asks the gatekeeper why the gate is barred and what quarrel lies behind it.
168.nuance: Line 4 (நீயிலையார் புதனடற்கு நிமித்தம்) is hard to divide; the reading takes it only as a question about the cause.

169.reading: The words of the woman who planted the branch are given: wanting someone to argue well with her about the grace the robed ascetics teach, she planted this naaval branch; let the gatekeeper do his duty, and if anyone has the wit, let them bring an answer in the great king's assembly.
169.event: The gatekeeper reports Kundalakesi's challenge: she planted the branch to call for a debate before the king's assembly.
169.nuance: The verse ends எனச் சொன்னாள், she said, after the gatekeeper's answer of 167, so it is read as Kundalakesi's challenge relayed to Neelakesi; it could also be read as spoken directly by a woman present at the gate. இலிங்கியர் (line 1), those who bear a sect's mark, is read as the Buddhist monks whose teaching she defends; the sense of அருள் here is not fixed.

170.reading: Neelakesi tells the gatekeeper that if so, the gate need be barred no longer, elephants and chariots may move as they will, and he should tell his king; saying this, she of the coral-red lips plucks up the naaval branch.
170.event: Neelakesi pulls up the challenge-branch, accepting Kundalakesi's challenge and reopening the king's gate.
170.nuance: Uprooting the branch is the formal acceptance of the debate, and it also frees the palace traffic: the debater's first effect is on public order.

links.note: Both use the sea of births: the Kural's பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல், crossed by reaching the Lord's feet; the Neelakesi's sea of the souls' own evil deeds, crossed on a raft the Jina made.
links.teaches: The Jain hymn fills in what the couplet leaves open: the sea is made of the swimmer's own deeds, and the Lord's part is to build the raft, not to hold the swimmer.

gains.a: the hymn's raft is seen answering a Tamil formula in which reaching the god is the only way across
gains.b: the couplet's bare verb 'reach the feet' is shown to admit a reading in which reaching means following a path one must travel oneself

links.note: Both say that the two kinds of deed, good and evil, leave the soul: in the Kural, for those who love the Lord's true praise; in the Neelakesi, by the way the Jina taught under the asoka tree.
links.teaches: Sung in the middle of Neelakesi's own praise, the verse credits release from both deeds to the teaching the Jina gave, not to the praise itself, which the couplet makes sufficient.

gains.a: the hymn's claim that merit too must go is matched by an older Tamil statement that both deeds are bonds
gains.b: the couplet's 'true praise' (பொருள்சேர் புகழ்) is shown being read as praise of a teaching to be followed

links.note: Both speak of the two deeds (இருவினை) and their ending: the Jina taught the way they part; Tirumular says that when they balance, grace-power comes as the guru and one's own doing ends.
links.teaches: On the same pair of deeds the Jain hymn gives the teacher only the role of telling the way, while Tirumular makes the guru a descent of grace that ends the soul's own agency.

gains.a: the hymn's silence about grace becomes visible as a position once set beside a text that makes grace the agent
gains.b: the Saiva doctrine of the balanced deeds is seen against a release in which no power descends and the soul does the work

links.note: Both praise the highest being as victor over Death: Siva kicked Death and became king of the south; the Jina passed beyond Death (காலனைக் கடந்தாய்) along with desire, aging and birth.
links.teaches: The same victory over Death means a deed of force against another being in the Saiva invocation and a leaving-behind of one's own mortal condition in the Jain hymn.

gains.a: the hymn's war imagery is seen as borrowed from a praise tradition that told the victory as combat
gains.b: the kick of the invocation is set against a victory that requires no enemy outside the self

links.note: Neelakesi's first charge against the Buddha is that he does not count eating flesh a fault; the couplet argues that flesh is sold only because people eat it.
links.teaches: The couplet supplies the reason a Jain debater can blame the flesh-eater who kills nothing: the eating is what causes the killing, so silence on eating is silence on killing.

gains.a: the bare charge in the verse gains the argument by which it is pressed later in the Neelakesi
gains.b: the couplet's market argument is seen aimed at a school's actual position in Tamil debate

links.note: Neelakesi charges that the Buddha does not count enduring austerity a vow; the Kundalakesi fragment calls bodily mortifications, nakedness among them, mere words, and puts tapas in restrained living.
links.teaches: The Buddhist fragment confirms the position the Jain debater attacks but shows it as a relocation of austerity into conduct, not the plain denial of austerity the charge describes.

gains.a: the Jain charge is seen against the opponent's own words
gains.b: the fragment's list of empty practices is shown to have a Jain target that the Neelakesi takes up

links.note: Neelakesi sets out to debate in order to do compassion (தயா செய்தற் பொருட்டாக); in the debate she asks whether one who let his own calf die has compassion (தயா) for others.
links.teaches: The debate is a contest over who owns compassion: the Jain debater's mission is framed as தயா, and her attack denies the Buddha the same virtue.

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before a king's assembly
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam's rubric (குண்டலகேசி வாதச் சருக்கம்); the id differs from vaadham, which the list already uses for alchemy

new_concepts.gloss: the vow; a religious observance or discipline undertaken
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word (163, நோன்பு என்னான்)
